name: Carlos Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and prepare accounts and tax returns for charities at a firm. I have done this for years and know the usual files, but a senior partner checks the harder cases. I use the approved AI assistant every day to sort receipts, then compare its guesses with invoices and bank entries. I like making a charity’s grant figures understandable, but chasing missing donation papers near filing time wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the home side of the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Leila, my partner, works at the public library, and our two school-age children make pickup a shared job. We have a mortgage, typical accountant pay and about four months of expenses saved. Some similar firms are nearby; I like trying useful tools early and I think staff should have a say when their hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to use any saved minutes to ring clients about missing receipts. A quick draft still needs a human to say which number is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have around four months of expenses saved and both wages cover the mortgage, so this picture feels stable for us. I would still worry if the firm used a tiny efficiency to stop teaching newer accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using the approved AI assistant I use every day to sort charity receipts, then check the bank entries myself. In the first year I would keep reviewing returns and bring one error to our weekly paid staff learning hour so the new starters can see the source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my pay, and a bit protective of the younger staff. We should not let a saved minute become a lost lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A community centre bought sports gear for children, and the assistant put it under office furniture. I checked the supplier invoice before the junior filed the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the paid learning hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is already on our rota, and everyone can attend without giving up an evening at home. My partner Leila works at the public library, so our school pickup is a shared puzzle.

I would keep a **human check** on every tax return.
think: Our **four-month cushion** and two wages make this a stable picture.
I worry a small efficiency may erase **junior learning**.
do: Keep using the **approved daily assistant** and compare charity receipts to bank entries.
Review returns and share an **error example** in the paid weekly learning hour.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and protective of newer accountants.

He treats the **paid learning hour** as part of ordinary work, not a collective campaign or unpaid favour.

steps.text: Keep reviewing charity accounts with approved AI and source bank checks
Share one source-checked error example in existing paid weekly staff learning hour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the partners to put the staffing changes and error counts on the table for everyone. If software drafts the returns, the firm should say how new people will learn to catch mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tax notes and checks take most of my day, so I could lose a paid day when the firm automates those tasks. Our four-month cushion gives us room to respond, but the mortgage depends on both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask our staff association to collect expected hours and vacant-post counts, then test the approved drafting tool on six closed charity returns during paid time with senior review. If my hours fall in the first year, I would apply to advertised local accountant posts only with written salary and hours no worse than mine, while keeping current paid hours until a confirmed start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut, but I can do something useful before it arrives. The data matters more than a reassuring speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the staff report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would count overtime, vacancies left empty and corrections to software drafts, without any client names. That would let us ask for paid training with actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek another firm if you know the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being quick with a tool does not guarantee this firm keeps my hours. I would take a real written offer, not a recruiter’s hopeful call.

I would defend **paid junior learning** as drafting software spreads.
think: My **tax-check hours** could shrink by a paid day.
Our **four-month reserve** gives room, but the mortgage needs wages.
do: Collect **vacancy and overtime** figures through the staff association.
Test **six closed returns** with approved drafting AI during paid senior review.
After lost hours, seek **advertised local accountant work** with written equal pay/hours while keeping wages until start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible hours cuts, with ways to respond.

fieldNote: His **staff association work** is specific: hours, vacancies and error counts, with client identities protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches our charity accounts and tax screens in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031. The firm should give staff notice and tell clients who signs the reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my desk checking to become cheaper elsewhere, and the firm may remove my post. Four months of savings cannot promise me another accounting wage when local firms cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the staff association to seek written notice and a dated plan for paid client-contact work. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply to advertised local accountant jobs with written salary and hours at least equal to mine; if none is open, I would request eligible income support and keep any paid file work the firm still offers while Leila and I review the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by a likely lost wage, even with four months saved. The children still need the school run paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Leila to work longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila’s library schedule includes school pickup twice a week, so extra hours need a confirmed paid rota and another safe pickup. I would not count those shifts until both are arranged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust a new client-contact job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there is a paid vacancy and the salary and hours are written down. Client conversations may also be automated, so I would not call that role permanent shelter.

I would seek **written staff notice** and named client sign-off.

S2.quote: Four months of savings cannot promise me another accounting wage when local firms cut together.
fieldNote: He does not treat **daily AI use** as job protection when full AGI reaches thinking work in 2028.

steps.text: Seek written cut notice through staff association before 2028
Apply to advertised accounting posts after job loss with written equal salary and hours
Request eligible income support after 2028 job loss if no suitable post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us years to see whether clients will pay for someone to explain their charity accounts. The robots around 2034 do not move our screen-work deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me ask for paid client meetings and build savings, but I still expect AI to take much of the tax checking by 2031. I would want proof that the charity boards pay for the human conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners to let me lead one paid monthly meeting with two charity boards and record whether they renew at a fee covering my hours. I would add 100 a month to our reserve while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if the firm cuts my tax hours, I would stay in salaried client work only if both boards renew at paid rates, or seek an advertised local accounting post with written equal pay and hours while keeping remaining paid files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk work but I can test a service over five years. A board’s thanks is not a payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would point to unpaid grants and explain why the cash balance differs from the budget. A senior partner would check my advice before the meeting ends, because I am competent but not the best technical reviewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse paid meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the tax work I have and ask for a written hours plan. I would not spend family evenings giving free board advice to prove demand.

I would remind staff **2034 robots** arrive after account-screen exposure.
think: Board **renewals** must fund paid client work before I rely on it.

After lost tax hours, stay only if **both boards renew** at salary-covering fees or seek local written equal-pay work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about desk losses, with time to test paid demand.
S3.quote: A board’s thanks is not a payslip.
fieldNote: His **paid service test** requires partner approval, senior review and two board renewals at fees covering his hours.
If meetings are **unfunded**, he keeps paid tax work rather than giving unpaid evening advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to strengthen family savings and build a service clients actually pay for. The robots around 2039 do not delay the tax desk change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might see the children older and our mortgage balance lower, if both incomes stay steady. My tax checking still faces AGI in 2036, so a paid board service has to prove its worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep current accounts and ask the partners for paid quarterly board meetings with senior review, if the boards agree to a fee. I would first build six months of expenses in cash with 130 monthly deposits while both wages hold, then pay extra principal; in the first year after 2036, if tax hours fall, I would stay only if the board fees fund my salary, or take an advertised local post with written pay and hours at least equal to now before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end while the next few years of wages look steady. I would still watch the mortgage account each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cash before extra principal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower loan balance cannot pay a surprise school bill or a missed library shift. Six months of cash would let us keep the children settled during a search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a public grant for the board service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm should charge clients for work they value. I would support public help for workers losing hours, but I would not present a commercial service as a charity project.

I would note **2039 robots** do not postpone the tax desk change.
think: My **tax checks** remain exposed in 2036 even if charity boards continue buying advice.
A **six-month cash buffer** needs both wages to stay steady.
do: Keep **accounts work** and test paid board meetings with partner, senior and client approval.

fieldNote: His **cash-first sequence** keeps liquidity for school or wage interruptions before extra mortgage payments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our tax and accounts screens could change before we can build a longer buffer. Written notice, paid client work and real vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches a new accountant to spot a wrong grant entry. A fast draft cannot explain itself to a charity board.

headlineQuote: A fast draft cannot explain itself to a charity board.
portrait: At **43**, Carlos is an experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles charity files.
He and **partner Leila** have two school-age children, a mortgage, typical pay and four months saved.
He uses **AI daily** with source checks and backs staff input on hours; some similar local firms exist.
The **2028 deadline** threatens tax checking, while longer runways allow paid board work and conditional savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his desk work before a longer household buffer is built.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, paid client work and real posted vacancies.
